catalog_quote: Ударение. Саамский язык имеет связанное ударение (главное) на первом слоге, что относится к произношению отдельных изолированных слов. Втростепенные [sic] ударения падают на другие нечетные слоги, кроме последнего. Все эти ударения - механические, результат периодического напряжения и ослабления мускулов, - они не влияют на смысловую сторону слова, акустически являясь, по-видимому, повышением основного тона (см. осциллограммы). Артикуляционно ударение - это большее напряжение голосовых связок. [p. 122] ... Взаимосвязанность структурных элементов слова основывается не только на взаимном влиянии соседних фонем, но и на единстве главного ударения, падающего на первый слог, и последующих второстепенных ударений, падающих, соответственно, на третий, пятый и другие слоги, кроме последнего. [p. 127]
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Kildin Saami is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Wilbur 2007 (Leipzig MA thesis, 'Syllable structures and stress patterns in Kildin Saami'), is exactly on topic but no copy could be found anywhere online (Glottolog record has no URL; both Joshua Wilbur ORCID profiles list zero works; Zenodo/LingBuzz/OSF/HELDA/Bielefeld PUB negative; The best modern description, Rießler 2022 (Oxford Guide to the Uralic Languages, pp. 219-239), has a self-archived submitted manuscript on the Helsinki Research Portal, but the file is behind an automated-access block that automated download, direct download, headless and headed (Xvfb) Chrome/Firefox and a reader proxy all failed to pass; OUP copy paywalled — priority high. The first-hand statement actually read is Kert 1971 p. 122 (already held by the project, scanned + image-verified): fixed non-contrastive primary stress on the first syllable, secondary stress on other odd-numbered syllables except the final one; Kert 1966 p. 157 (loanword exception) and Kert 1993 p. 137 agree. Kuruch 1985 sketch and Rießler 2013 (downloaded) are silent on stress; Rießler 2007 (borrowing) and Egorov & Burov 2026 (voiceless sonorants, abstract read) are paywalled and not about word stress.

new_statements.translation: The Saami language has bound (main) stress on the first syllable, which pertains to the pronunciation of individual isolated words. Secondary stresses fall on the other odd-numbered syllables, except the last. All these stresses are mechanical, the result of periodic tensing and relaxing of the muscles; they do not affect the meaning of the word, being acoustically, apparently, a rise in fundamental tone (see the oscillograms). Articulatorily, stress is greater tension of the vocal folds.
new_statements.citation: Kert, G. M. 1971. Saamskij jazyk (kil'dinskij dialekt): fonetika, morfologija, sintaksis. Leningrad: Nauka.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is fixed on the word-initial syllable (non-contrastive); secondary stresses fall on subsequent odd-numbered syllables (3rd, 5th..) but never on the word-final syllable. Kert 1966 p.157 adds that loanwords are excepted from initial main stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicit: secondary stresses on the other odd-numbered syllables except the last (p.122); p.127 spells it out as 'на третий, пятый и другие слоги, кроме последнего' (on the 3rd, 5th and other syllables, except the last); same in Kert 1993 §2.1.2 and Kert 1966 p.157. Kert 1971 p.123 adds that several degrees of (secondary) stress probably exist, by analogy with Äimä's Inari data and auditory impression, pending experimental study.
new_statements.exceptions: Kert 1971: none for isolated words; notes that stress distribution of words spoken in a phrase differs from isolated words, and that logical (emphatic) stress exists. Kert 1966 p.157: main stress initial 'за исключением заимствованных слов' (except in borrowed words).
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly the isolated/citation-form word ('относится к произношению отдельных изолированных слов'); phrase-level distribution said to differ (p.123). Stress is stated to be non-contrastive ('не влияют на смысловую сторону слова'). Supported by the author's oscillographic amplitude comparisons of stressed vs unstressed vowels (pp.122-123, 127).
new_statements.identity_note: Kert 1971 is explicitly a description of the Kildin dialect (kild1236) of Kola Saami, based on the author's fieldwork and oscillographic measurements; Kert 1966 (p.156) and Kert 1993 (p.135) are titled 'Saamskij jazyk' generally but both state the sketch is written on the basis of the Kildin dialect. Kert 1971 p.123 cites Äimä's Inari Saami (inar1241) five-degree phrase-stress typology only as an analogy, not as Kildin data.

new_statements.quote: Саамский язык имеет связанное ударение (главное) на первом слоге, что относится к произношению отдельных изолированных слов. Второстепенные ударения падают на другие нечетные слоги, кроме последнего. Все эти ударения - механические, результат периодического напряжения и ослабления мускулов, - они не влияют на смысловую сторону слова, акустически являясь, по-видимому, повышением основного тона (см. осциллограммы). new_statements.translation: Saami has fixed (main) stress on the first syllable, which applies to the pronunciation of individual isolated words. Secondary stresses fall on the other odd-numbered syllables except the last. All these stresses are mechanical, the result of periodic tensing and relaxing of the muscles; they do not affect the semantic side of the word, acoustically being, apparently, a rise of the fundamental pitch (see the oscillograms). Articulatorily, stress is greater tension of the vocal cords.
new_statements.citation: Kert, G. M. 1971. Saamskij jazyk (kil'dinskij dialekt): fonetika, morfologija, sintaksis. Leningrad: Nauka.

new_statements.reading: Fixed, non-contrastive word-initial primary stress; secondary stress on subsequent odd-numbered syllables, never on the final syllable (i.e. trochaic left-to-right footing with final-syllable exclusion). Kert 1966 (p. 157) adds a loanword exception; Kert 1993 (p. 137) restates the same rule. This is the author's own instrumental (oscillographic) study of the Kildin dialect, hence first-hand.
new_statements.found_by: works with stress in the title

new_statements.quote: [p. 223, 13.2.3] There are no word-level distinctions based on suprasegmental phenomena in Kildin Saami. [p. 223, 13.2.5] Relevant word-prosodic domains beyond the segment level are syllable, foot, and (phonological) word. The latter is the domain of word stress, while foot is the domain of morphophonological processes (13.3.1). [p. 224] Wilbur (2007) has shown that different syllable structures and the distribution of stress patterns in Kildin Saami complement one another in focusing on the initial syllable of a foot. The domain of stress is the phonological word, where the first syllable always carries the main stress. Word stems can be disyllabic or monosyllabic stress groups, with the latter type being considerably more common, and always carrying main stress. In morphologically complex words, secondary stress can occur on one or more syllables.
new_statements.citation: Rießler, Michael. 2022. Kildin Saami. In: M. Bakró-Nagy, J. Laakso & E. Skribnik (eds.), The Oxford Guide to the Uralic Languages, 219-239. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: text layer, chapter footer 'DOI: 10.1093/oso/9780198767664.003.0013', header 'Chapter 13 Kildin Saami, Michael Rießler'). Extracted PDF pp. 5-6 (printed 223-224) with extracted text. Every quoted sentence is there verbatim: p. 223 section 13.2.3 Suprasegmentals: 'There are no word-level distinctions based on suprasegmental phenomena in Kildin Saami.'; p. 223 section 13.2.4 Phonotactics: 'Long vowels or diphthongs and long consonants occur only in (primarily or secondarily) stressed syllables.'; p. 223 section 13.2.5 Prosody: 'Relevant word-prosodic domains beyond the segment level are syllable, foot, and (phonological) word. The latter is the domain of word stress, while foot is the domain…
new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog (initial stress) and with Kert 1971/1966/1993 on fixed initial main stress. Adds that stress is non-contrastive (no word-level suprasegmental distinctions), that the foot is the morphophonological domain with stress focused on its initial syllable, that compounds follow the same rule, and that long vowels/diphthongs/geminates are confined to stressed syllables. It is less specific than Kert on secondary stress ('one or more syllables' in complex words vs. Kert's odd-numbered non-final syllables); no contradiction. Note: the catalog's open_url (the Harvard library catalogue record cdi_ceeol_journals_897111) resolves to a different item, Rießler 2020 'Rimma Kuruch and…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main word stress always falls on the first syllable of the phonological word; stress is not contrastive (no word-level suprasegmental distinctions). Stems form mono- or disyllabic stress groups (feet) whose initial syllable is stressed; long vowels, diphthongs and long consonants occur only in stressed (primary or secondary) syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'In morphologically complex words, secondary stress can occur on one or more syllables' (p. 224); no odd-syllable or non-final rule is stated. 13.2.4 (p. 223): 'Long vowels or diphthongs and long consonants occur only in (primarily or secondarily) stressed syllables.'
new_statements.exceptions: None for placement. 'Regarding word stress, morphological compounds follow the rules just described' (p. 224), i.e. compounds are stressed like simple words; the author notes that what constitutes a phonological word (13.3.9) 'is not well understood yet'.
new_statements.identity_note: Rießler 2022 describes Kildin Saami as a whole (four surviving dialects: Kiillt, Kårdegg, Lujaaʹvvr, Arsjogg), based on the author's own investigation with Lovozero consultants; no dialect-specific stress differences are mentioned. The catalog's open_url for work 0 actually points to Rießler 2020 (Linguistica Uralica 56(3): 220-225, a language-planning note on Rimma Kuruch), a different item from the listed chapter.

sources.quote: This is the first English-language description of Kildin Saami and the basic features of its phonology, morphology, and syntax. Kildin Saami is a critically endangered indigenous language of the Kola Peninsula in north-west Russia, with only about 100 active speakers. It is characterized by a complex phonology, a remarkably rich inventory of consonant phonemes and a highly fusional inflectional morphology [...]
sources.note: Most recent authoritative English-language description by the leading Kildin specialist; its phonology section would confirm or refine Kert's initial-stress + alternating-secondary statement (and the loanword exception) in modern terms.

sources.quote: Главное ударение, за исключением заимствованных слов, падает на первый слог, второстепенное — на следующий нечетный слог, кроме последнего. Связанность ударения создает особую структуру слова, при которой долгота согласных слова тесно связана с долготой гласных. [tr.: Main stress, except in loanwords, falls on the first syllable, secondary stress on the next odd syllable except the last. The fixedness of stress creates a special word structure in which consonant length is closely tied to vowel length.]

sources.note: printed p.157 (PDF p.156), end of §4: 'Главное ударение, за исключением заимствованных слов, падает на первый слог, второстепенное — на следующий нечетный слог, кроме последнего. Связанность ударения создает особую структуру слова..' — main stress on the first syllable except in loanwords; secondary on the next odd syllable except the last; bound stress ties consonant length to vowel length. p.156: sketch based on the Kildin dialect.
Nothing on stress/prosody; bibliography lists Kert 1961, Kert 1971, Kuruch et al. 1985, Rießler '13. Kildin Saami' (ResearchGate preprint), Scheller 2010/2024.
